query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small, controlled amount of aluminum (≈3 at.%) to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will promote in situ formation of a thin, adherent Al2O3 scale during high-temperature exposure, thereby greatly enhancing its resistance to oxygen attack (pesting) while largely preserving its room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% ductility at room temperature and yield strengths of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but with inadequate oxygen resistance due to uncontrolled oxidation.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 3 at.% Al as a microalloying addition into the HfNbTaTiZr alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Expose the Al-modified alloy to air at 800 °C for 5 hours under strain rate conditions of 10−4–10−2 s−1, similar to the baseline mechanical testing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, slow-growing and adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: At high temperature, Al diffuses to the surface and oxidizes preferentially to form a protective Al2O3 layer, which slows oxygen ingress and substrate oxidation. This barrier minimizes pesting without significantly altering the bulk phase or mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Al-alloyed variant will show markedly reduced oxidation (e.g., less mass gain and spallation, stable scale formation) at 800 °C over 5 hours, while retaining tensile ductility in the 8–16% range at room temperature and maintaining yield strength in the high-temperature regime.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which displays acceptable mechanical properties but suffers from rapid oxidation (pesting) under high-temperature air exposure.
generation.boundary: This intervention is predicted to be effective under moderate high-temperature conditions (around 800 °C for durations up to 5 hours in air) and at strain rates typical of service conditions; behavior at significantly higher temperatures or prolonged exposures remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Al concentration might require fine-tuning to avoid potential embrittlement or phase changes, and the long-term adhesion and integrity of the alumina scale under cyclic thermal or mechanical loads needs further evaluation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of cast samples: one set of conventional equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and a second set modified with ≈3 at.% Al. Subject both sets to air exposure at 800 °C for 5 hours. After oxidation, analyze the surface scales (using SEM and XRD) and perform mechanical tensile tests at room temperature and at elevated temperatures.
measurements: Surface oxide scale morphology and phase identification (to confirm the presence of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 layer)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-modified samples do not develop a continuous Al2O3 scale (as confirmed by microscopy and XRD) or if they exhibit no significant reduction in oxidation (mass gain, spallation) and/or a degradation in room-temperature or high-temperature mechanical properties compared to the unmodified samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

A Study of the Effects of Al, Cr, Hf, and Ti Additions on the Microstructure and Oxidation of Nb-24Ti-18Si Silicide Based Alloys

Abstract: AbstractIn Nb-silicide based alloys Al, Cr, Hf, and Ti additions are crucial for achieving balance of properties. It is not known how the simultaneous addition of Hf with Al and Ti, or Hf with Al, Cr, and Ti affects macrosegregation, and how the alloying affects hardness, Young’s modulus and bulk alloy oxidation, and contamination of the solid solution Nbss and the Nb5Si3 compound by oxygen. Two alloys with nominal compositions (at.%) Nb-24Ti-18Si-5Al-5Hf (alloy NbSiTiHf-5Al) and Nb-24Ti-18Si-5Al-5Cr-5Hf (alloy NbSiTiHf-5Al-5Cr) were studied in the as-cast and heat-treated conditions and after isothermal oxidation at 800 and 1200 °C and were compared with similar alloys without Hf. In both alloys there was macrosegregation of Si and Ti, which was more severe in NbSiTiHf-5Al. Both alloys formed Nbss+βNb5Si3 eutectic. The Nbss was stable and its Al and Cr concentrations increased with increasing Ti concentration. Microstructures and Isothermal Oxidation of the Alumina Scale Forming Nb1.45Si2.7Ti2.25Al3.25Hf0.35 and Nb1.35Si2.3Ti2.3Al3.7Hf0.35 Alloys

Abstract: AbstractCoating system(s) will be required for Nb-silicide based alloys. Alumina forming alloys that are chemically compatible with the Nb-silicide based alloy substrate could be components of such systems. The intermetallic alloys Nb1.45Si2.7Ti2.25Al3.25Hf0.35 (MG5) and Nb1.35Si2.3Ti2.3Al3.7Hf0.35 (MG6) were studied in the cast, heat treated and isothermally oxidised conditions at 800 and 1200 °C to find out if they are αAl2O3 scale formers. A (Al/Si)alloy versus Nb/(Ti + Hf)alloy map, which can be considered to be a map for Multi-Principle Element or Complex Concentrated Nb-Ti-Si-Al-Hf alloys, and a [Nb/(Ti + Hf)]Nb5Si3 versus [Nb/(Ti + Hf)]alloy map were constructed making use of the alloy design methodology NICE and data from a previously studied alloy, and were used to select the alloys MG5 and MG6 that were expected (i) not to pest, (ii) to form αAl2O3 scale at 1200 °C, (iii) to have no solid solution, (iv) to form only hexagonal Nb5Si3 and (v) to have microstructures consisting of hexagonal Nb5Si3, Ti5Si3, Ti5Si4, TiSi silicide
